draft.title: Mise-en-scène and lighting
card: This is everything placed in the frame: the setting, props, costume and the positions of the actors. A director chooses each one to show something about the story or a character.
Costume and props can show who a character is. A scuffed school bag and a torn jacket suggest a character who is struggling or careless.
Position in the frame can show relationships. A character placed alone at the edge of an empty frame can seem cut off from others.
Light sets the mood. Harsh light with deep shadows can feel tense or threatening. Soft, warm light can feel calm or gentle.
draft.remember: Everything in the frame is a choice, and the lighting tells the viewer how to feel about it.

a.q: Which of these is part of a film's mise-en-scène?
opts: A character's costume and the props around them
A score that plays over a chase scene
The speed at which the shots are cut together
The angle the camera uses to look down
a.why: Mise-en-scène is everything placed in the frame, so costume and props belong to it. A score is sound, cutting speed is editing and camera angle is a camera choice. None of these is placed in the frame.
a.clue: Think of what you could point to inside the picture.

b.q: In a scene, Tariq sits alone in a dim room lit by one harsh lamp that throws deep shadows across his face. What mood does the lighting most likely create?
opts: Tension or unease
Calm and comfort
Joy and celebration
Boredom and routine
b.why: Harsh light with deep shadows usually feels tense or threatening, so the lighting suggests unease. Calm and comfort would come from soft, warm light, which is the opposite of what is described here.
b.clue: Compare harsh shadows with soft light.

a.best: A character's costume and the props around them
